etymology: From Old French essaier, “to try, test, attempt,” through Late Latin exagium, a weighing or trial; the same root that gives the assayer his testing of metals. In the KJV it renders Hebrew nāsāh (to try, prove, attempt) and Greek peirazō (to attempt, essay).
biblical_def: To assay is to attempt, to essay, to try the doing of a thing—often a hard or untested thing—and the word carries the flavour of a trial made without prior proof. When Saul, newly converted, came to Jerusalem, he assayed to join himself to the disciples (Act 9:26); the verb marks the venture of a man not yet trusted, reaching toward a fellowship that feared him. Moses asks Israel whether God ever assayed to go and take him a nation from the midst of another nation (Deu 4:34)—an attempt unheard of in the annals of the nations, and one the LORD alone accomplished. David, buckled into Saul’s armour, assayed to go; for he had not proved it (1Sa 17:39), and finding the untried harness a hindrance, put it off to meet Goliath in the proven simplicity of sling and stone. Elihu’s companions ask, If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? (Job 4:2)—the tender approach of men venturing speech to a sufferer. The word therefore teaches holy venture: Saul’s reaching for the church, David’s refusal to fight in unproved armour, God’s unexampled assaying to redeem a people to Himself. Faith is not presumption, yet neither is it paralysis; it assays great things at the LORD’s bidding, proving in the doing what could not be proved beforehand, and leaving the untried armour of the flesh behind.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ASSAY as to try, attempt, or endeavour; to make trial of; and, in metallurgy, to examine an ore or metal to determine its purity.
webster_full: ASSAY, v.t. — To try; to attempt; to endeavour; to make an effort toward the doing of a thing. He assayed to go; for he had not proved it (1Sa 17:39).
ASSAY, v.t. — To prove or examine by trial; to test the quality or worth of a thing before venturing upon it.
ASSAY, v.t. — In metallurgy, to examine an ore or metallic substance by chemical or other means to ascertain the proportion of pure metal it contains.
ASSAY, n. — The trial or examination itself; the determination of the quantity of pure metal in an ore or alloy; hence, any first attempt or essay.
ASSAYER, n. — One who assays; an officer appointed to try the purity and weight of metals, especially of coin and bullion.
scriptures: Act 9:26
And when Saul was come to Jerusalem, he assayed to join himself to the disciples: but they were all afraid of him, and believed not that he was a disciple.
Deu 4:34

Or hath God assayed to go and take him a nation from the midst of another nation, by temptations, by signs, and by wonders, and by war, and by a mighty hand, and by a stretched out arm, and by great terrors, according to all that the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?
And David girded his sword upon his armour, and he assayed to go; for he had not proved it. And David said unto Saul, I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them. And David put them off him.
Job 4:2
If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? but who can withhold himself from speaking?
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a lost verb of holy venture; it recovers the difference between faith that attempts great things at God’s bidding and the flesh that either presumes without proving or refuses to move at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The age that has forgotten assay is not short of attempters—it is loud with self-styled venturers who assay every enterprise except the one that matters, the joining of themselves to the people of God and the proving of the promises by obedience. Saul assayed to join the disciples; the modern professor assays to remain at a comfortable distance, admiring the church without venturing into her fellowship, its risks, its costs. And where men will not assay the hard obedience of faith, they yet presume the untried armour of the flesh—David’s refusal rebukes it: he would not go out in harness he had not proved. The word calls the timid to venture and the presumptuous to prove, and reserves the greatest assaying to God, who alone attempted, and accomplished, the taking of a nation to Himself out of the midst of the nations.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the biblical posture of holy venture: faith that assays great things because God has commanded them, without demanding to see the end before it will begin, yet refusing the unproved armour of the flesh. David laid off Saul’s harness and took the proven sling; Saul of Tarsus assayed the fellowship that feared him and was at last received; and behind both stands the God who assayed the unexampled work of redemption. To assay in this sense is to obey before one can fully explain, to step out on the bare word of the LORD, and to prove in the doing what could never be proved from the safety of the shore.
roots_summary: Old French essaier / Late Latin exagium (a weighing, trial) — to try, attempt, prove; rendering Hebrew nāsāh and Greek peirazō, the venturing of an untried thing.
roots_lines: Old French essaier — to try, test, attempt; the source of both assay and essay, which were once the same word.
Late Latin exagium — a weighing or trial (from exigere, to weigh out, examine), giving the metallurgist’s sense of testing purity.
Hebrew nāsāh (H5254) — to test, try, prove, attempt (Deu 4:34, God assaying to take Him a nation; 1Sa 17:39, David assaying to go).
Greek peirazō (G3985) — to attempt, essay, make trial of (Act 9:26; 16:7; 24:6, of assaying an undertaking).
English essay — the doublet of assay, preserving the sense of an attempt or first trial in prose.
usage: He assayed to go; for he had not proved it—David laid off the unproved armour and met Goliath with the sling he had proven, a rebuke to every trust in the untried harness of the flesh.
Saul assayed to join himself to the disciples: the convert’s holy venture toward a fellowship that at first feared him, until Barnabas vouched for the grace of God in him.
God alone assayed to go and take him a nation from the midst of another nation—an attempt without precedent among the nations, accomplished by a mighty hand and a stretched out arm.

etymology: From Old French eschiver, “to shun, avoid, flee from,” itself from a Frankish/Old High German root skiuhan, to dread or shrink from (the same root that gives modern shy and shun). In the KJV it renders Hebrew sūr (to turn aside, depart from) and Greek ekklinō (to turn away from).
biblical_def: To eschew is to turn aside from, to shun, to shrink away from as from a loathed thing—a stronger word than merely to avoid, for it carries the recoil of dread. It is the settled verb of Job’s character: that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil (Job 1:1), and twice the LORD Himself repeats the commendation to Satan—a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil (Job 1:8; 2:3). The pairing is exact and instructive: the fear of God and the eschewing of evil rise and fall together, for reverence toward the Holy One breeds recoil from what He hates. Job does not merely refrain from evil as one who calculates its costs; he shrinks from it as one who loves God shrinks from what would grieve Him. Peter gathers the same posture into the imperative of the whole Christian walk: Let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and ensue it (1Pe 3:11)—a turning from and a turning toward, a fleeing and a following. To eschew is thus the negative side of holiness, inseparable from its positive side: the same fear that makes a man depart from iniquity makes him pursue righteousness. Where the fear of God is lost, the recoil from evil is lost with it, and men grow bold in the very things from which the upright shrink.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ESCHEW as to flee from; to shun; to avoid, as something wrong, hurtful, or disgusting.
webster_full: ESCHEW, v.t. — To flee from; to shun; to seek to avoid; to keep at a distance from, as from something evil, hurtful, or offensive. One that feared God, and eschewed evil (Job 1:1).
ESCHEW, v.t. — To decline; to abstain from; to have nothing to do with, from a settled aversion of the mind.
ESCHEW, v.t. — To turn aside from a course or thing, as one shrinks from what he dreads or abhors.
ESCHEWER, n. — One who shuns or avoids; one who habitually turns from what is evil.
ESCHEWING, ppr. — Shunning; avoiding; fleeing from; declining, as from a thing dreaded or abhorred.
scriptures: Job 1:1
There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.
Job 1:8
And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?
Job 2:3

And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause.
Let him eschew evil, and do good; let him seek peace, and ensue it.
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine under dispute but a lost strength of aversion; it recovers the recoil from evil that the fear of God breeds, in an age that has taught men to tolerate, explore, and be curious about what the upright shrink from.
corruption_paragraphs: The temper of the age is precisely the opposite of eschewing. Where Job shrank from evil as from a loathed thing, the modern conscience is trained to be broad-minded toward it, to explore it, to withhold judgment, to call recoil itself a kind of narrowness. The very reflex of dread before sin—the flinching of a heart that fears God—is dismissed as squeamishness or hate. But Scripture ties the two together and will not let them part: one that feared God, and eschewed evil. Lose the fear of God and the eschewing goes with it; men grow easy and curious and at last companionable with the things from which the holy shrink. The word rebukes the flattering counsel that a mature faith must lose its recoil; it insists rather that the more a man loves the Holy One, the more violently he turns from what would grieve Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unbreakable link between reverence and aversion. To fear God is to hate what He hates, and to hate evil is to eschew it—to turn aside, to shun, to shrink away—not merely to refrain when it is costly. Peter joins the negative to the positive: eschew evil, and do good; seek peace, and ensue it. Holiness is this double motion, a fleeing and a following, and the man who has lost the flee will soon lose the follow. Cultivate again the tender conscience that recoils; it is not weakness but the fear of God made visible in a life.
roots_summary: Old French eschiver / Frankish skiuhan (to dread, shrink from) — to shun, flee from; rendering Hebrew sūr (turn aside) and Greek ekklinō, the recoil of a God-fearing heart from evil.
roots_lines: Old French eschiver — to shun, avoid, flee from; the immediate source of the English verb.
Frankish / Old High German skiuhan — to dread, shrink back; the same root behind modern shy and shun.
Hebrew sūr (H5493) — to turn aside, depart, remove; used of departing from evil (Job 1:1; Pro 3:7; 16:6).
Greek ekklinō (G1578) — to turn away from, avoid, eschew (1Pe 3:11; Rom 3:12; 16:17).
English shy, shun — the surviving native cousins of the same Germanic root, keeping the sense of shrinking away.
usage: One that feared God, and eschewed evil—the two clauses are one character; the reverence and the recoil cannot be separated in an upright man.
Peter’s double command: eschew evil, and do good; seek peace, and ensue it—a turning from and a turning toward, the whole motion of the sanctified life.
The age counsels tolerance and curiosity where Scripture counsels eschewing; the tender conscience that shrinks from evil is not narrowness but the fear of God made visible.

etymology: From Old English wrāþ, “angry, incensed, wrathful,” kin to wríþan, to writhe or twist—anger as the twisting or writhing of the mind. The predicate adjective of the noun wrath; it renders Hebrew chārāh (to burn, be kindled) and qātsaph (to be wroth).
biblical_def: Wroth is the old adjective of anger—to be wroth is to be incensed, kindled, hot with displeasure—and it is the writhing of the mind against what it will not bear. Its very first appearance is a warning: when the LORD had not respect to Cain’s offering, Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell (Gen 4:5), and the wrath of the rejected worshipper hardened swiftly into the murder of his brother. Jacob was wroth, and chode with Laban (Gen 31:36), the just indignation of a man long defrauded. Herod, mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth and slew the innocents of Bethlehem (Mat 2:16)—the fury of threatened power turned against the children. And in the Lord’s own parable the master, hearing of the unmerciful servant, was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors (Mat 18:34), a wrath that is wholly righteous and figures the just anger of God against the forgiven soul who will not forgive. So the word holds both a warning and a comfort. In man, wrath is mostly the flesh writhing at injury or affront, and Cain and Herod show whither it runs when unbridled—to blood. Yet there is a wrath that is holy: the settled displeasure of God against sin, slow, just, and terrible. Scripture bids us be ye angry, and sin not: the Christian is to eschew the wrath of Cain and to tremble before the wrath of the King, fleeing to the blood of Christ, which alone quenches the wrath we have deserved.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WROTH as very angry; much exasperated; incensed.
webster_full: WROTH, a. — Very angry; much exasperated; incensed; hot with displeasure. Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell (Gen 4:5).
WROTH, a. — Moved to indignation, whether justly, as at a wrong endured, or unjustly, as in the fury of wounded pride.
WROTH, a. — Kindled in mind against a person or thing; stirred to the writhing displeasure that the word originally named.
WROTH, a. — Used of God, the settled and righteous displeasure of the Holy One against sin (Deu 1:34; Isa 57:17).
WROTH — A predicate adjective, closely allied to the noun WRATH, and now nearly obsolete except in the language of Scripture.
scriptures: Gen 4:5
But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.
And Jacob was wroth, and chode with Laban: and Jacob answered and said to Laban, What is my trespass? what is my sin, that thou hast so hotly pursued after me?
Mat 2:16

Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men.
And his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due unto him.
corruption_summary: Not a redefined term but a word that exposes two errors of the age at once: the sentimentalism that denies God is ever wroth, and the license that excuses the wrath of Cain in man.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern temper commits two opposite faults, and wroth rebukes them both. On the one hand it will not have a God who is wroth—wrath is thought unworthy of love, and the settled displeasure of the Holy One against sin is edited out, leaving a deity too soft to save. Yet Scripture makes the Lord of the parable wroth at the unforgiving servant, and the whole gospel presupposes a real wrath from which men must be delivered. On the other hand the age excuses the wrath of Cain in man—the writhing rage of wounded pride that runs, unchecked, to violence of tongue and hand. Cain was very wroth and slew his brother; Herod was exceeding wroth and slew the children. The flesh baptizes its fury as righteous cause, and calls its writhing zeal. The word will let neither error stand: God’s wrath is real and just; man’s wrath is mostly the flesh, and deadly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. First, confess the wrath of God as an article of the faith and a mercy of the gospel: his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors—a warning to every forgiven soul who will not forgive, and a reason to flee to the blood of Christ, in whom alone the deserved wrath is quenched. Second, mortify the wrath of Cain: be ye angry, and sin not; let not the sun go down upon your wrath. The believer is to fear the one wrath and forsake the other—to tremble before the righteous displeasure of the King, and to slay in himself the hot, writhing anger that fells a brother and dims the countenance.
roots_summary: Old English wrāþ (angry), kin to wríþan (to writhe) — anger as the twisting of the mind; rendering Hebrew chārāh (to burn) and qātsaph (to be wroth).
roots_lines: Old English wrāþ — angry, incensed, wrathful; the predicate adjective allied to the noun wrāþþu, wrath.
Old English wríþan — to writhe, twist, bind; picturing anger as the writhing or twisting of the mind.
Hebrew chārāh (H2734) — to burn, be kindled, grow hot with anger (Gen 4:5, Cain very wroth; 31:36, Jacob wroth).
Hebrew qātsaph (H7107) — to be wroth, break out in anger (Gen 41:10; Lev 10:16; Deu 1:34).
English wrath, writhe — the surviving native kin, keeping the sense of burning displeasure and twisting distress.
usage: Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell—the first wrath in Scripture, and a warning of whither the flesh’s fury runs when a rejected worshipper will not master it.
Herod was exceeding wroth and slew the innocents: the rage of threatened power turned against children, the wrath of Cain enthroned.
His lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors—the righteous wrath of the King against the forgiven soul who will not forgive, a warning to flee to the blood of Christ.

etymology: From Old French descrier, “to cry out, proclaim, announce,” hence to spy out and give report of; some trace a blending with descrire (to describe). In the KJV it is the single-verse rendering of Hebrew tūr / the sense of spying out and reconnoitring a place.
biblical_def: To descry is to spy out, to reconnoitre, to catch sight of and report—the scout’s work of discovering a place before the host moves against it. The word stands but once in the whole KJV: the house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel (Jdg 1:23), sending men to spy out the city (once called Luz) before taking it, and the spies’ kindness to an informer opened the gate. Rare as the verb is, the deed it names runs through the Scriptures like a thread. The LORD Himself commands the reconnaissance of the promised land: Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan (Num 13:2), and Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan (Num 13:17)—a descrying that ended in unbelief when ten of the twelve saw giants and forgot the promise. Joshua later sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly (Jos 2:1), and their descrying of Jericho met the faith of Rahab, whose scarlet line and confession saved her house. So the descrier’s errand is neither idle nor faithless in itself; the sin at Kadesh was not the spying but the seeing without faith, measuring the giants and not the God who gave the land. To descry rightly is to reconnoitre the field of obedience with the eye of faith—to see the walls and the giants truly, and the LORD more truly still, going up at once because He that promised is able.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DESCRY as to espy; to explore; to examine by the eye; to detect or discover something distant or concealed.
webster_full: DESCRY, v.t. — To espy; to detect; to discover at a distance something before hidden or not clearly seen. The house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel (Jdg 1:23).
DESCRY, v.t. — To explore; to examine and view, as a scout or spy who reconnoitres a place before an army advances.
DESCRY, v.t. — To discover or perceive, as an object dimly seen or partly concealed; to make out with the eye.
DESCRY, n. — Discovery; a thing descried; the sight or detection of what was distant or hidden.
DESCRIER, n. — One who descries, espies, or discovers; a scout or discoverer.
scriptures: Jdg 1:23
And the house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel. (Now the name of the city before was Luz.)
Num 13:2
Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them.
And Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan, and said unto them, Get you up this way southward, and go up into the mountain:
Jos 2:1
And Joshua the son of Nun sent out of Shittim two men to spy secretly, saying, Go view the land, even Jericho. And they went, and came into an harlot's house, named Rahab, and lodged there.
corruption_summary: A KJV hapax, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the difference between reconnoitring the field of obedience with the eye of faith and the faithless seeing that measures the giants and forgets the God who gave the land.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the word rebukes is the sin of the ten spies—to descry the land and see only the giants. The men sent to spy out Canaan reported truly of the walled cities and the sons of Anak, and their true report became a lie because it left God out of the reckoning. This is the abiding snare of the anxious heart: to survey the obstacles of obedience with an accurate eye and a faithless one, to count the difficulties and never the promises, and so to melt the courage of the whole camp. Caleb and Joshua descried the same giants and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able. The difference was not in the eyes but in the faith behind them. To descry rightly is to see the field truly, giants and all, and the LORD who gave it more truly still.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faith’s reconnaissance—the sober counting of the cost that Christ enjoins, joined to the confident reckoning of the God who cannot fail. The house of Joseph descried Bethel and took it; Joshua’s spies descried Jericho and found Rahab’s faith already at work behind the walls; and the LORD Himself commanded the searching of the land He had already given. There is no virtue in a blind venture, and none in a faithless survey. Look before you go up—and then, having seen the giants, go up at once, because He that promised is able to perform.
roots_summary: Old French descrier (to cry out, proclaim, spy out) — to espy, reconnoitre, discover; the KJV hapax at Jdg 1:23, kin to the spying out of the land in Numbers and Joshua.
roots_lines: Old French descrier — to cry out, proclaim, and hence to spy out and give report; the source of English descry.
Latin quiritare / discria- — underlying the sense of raising a cry, from which the notion of announcing a discovery derives.
Hebrew tūr (H8446) — to spy out, explore, search out (Num 13:2, 17, of searching the land of Canaan).
Hebrew rāgal (H7270) — to go about on foot as a spy, to reconnoitre (Jos 2:1, Joshua’s two men spying Jericho).
English describe — a near cousin through the same field of proclaiming and setting forth what is seen.
usage: The house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel—the KJV’s single use of the verb, the scouts’ work of spying out a city before the host went up.
The ten spies descried the land and saw only the giants; Caleb and Joshua descried the same giants and said, we are well able—the difference lay not in the eyes but in the faith behind them.
Joshua’s two men descried Jericho and found Rahab’s faith already at work; the descrier’s errand met the scarlet line that saved a house.

etymology: From Old French desconfit, past participle of desconfire, “to defeat, destroy, undo,” from Latin dis- (undo) + conficere (to make, accomplish, finish off): literally to un-make, to finish off an enemy in battle. In the KJV it renders Hebrew hāmam (to rout, throw into confusion) and kindred verbs of overthrow.
biblical_def: To discomfit is to rout, to overthrow, to defeat utterly and throw into confusion—a battlefield word for the undoing of an army, not the mere ruffling of a mind (its weakened modern sense). Almost always in Scripture the discomfiting is the LORD’s own act. At Rephidim, Joshua discomfited Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword (Exo 17:13)—yet the victory hung upon Moses’ uplifted hands on the hill, so that the sword below prevailed only while intercession held above. Against Sisera, the LORD discomfited Sisera, and all his chariots, and all his host (Jdg 4:15), and the mighty captain fled away on his feet before Barak. David sings of the same divine rout: God sent out arrows, and scattered them; lightning, and discomfited them (2Sa 22:15), the heavens themselves enlisted against the foe. And Isaiah foretells the fall of Assyria by no human sword: he shall flee, and his young men shall be discomfited (Isa 31:8). The pattern is unbroken and deeply comforting: the discomfiting of God’s enemies is His work, wrought sometimes through Joshua’s sword and Moses’ hands, sometimes by hailstone and lightning and sheer terror, but always by the LORD of hosts. His people fight, but He gives the rout; the battle is the LORD’s, and the enemy He undertakes to un-make is undone indeed.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DISCOMFIT as to rout; to defeat; to scatter in fight; to cause to flee; to vanquish and overthrow.
webster_full: DISCOMFIT, v.t. — To rout; to defeat; to scatter in fight; to cause to flee; to vanquish. Joshua discomfited Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword (Exo 17:13).
DISCOMFIT, v.t. — To overthrow; to break up and put to confusion, as an army or a host in battle.
DISCOMFIT, v.t. — To defeat the plans or purposes of; to frustrate; to undo utterly.
DISCOMFITURE, n. — Rout; defeat; overthrow; the breaking up and dispersion of an army; a total frustration.
DISCOMFITED, pp. — Routed; defeated; scattered; overthrown; put to confusion in battle.
scriptures: And Joshua discomfited Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.
Jdg 4:15
And the LORD discomfited Sisera, and all his chariots, and all his host, with the edge of the sword before Barak; so that Sisera lighted down off his chariot, and fled away on his feet.
And he sent out arrows, and scattered them; lightning, and discomfited them.
Isa 31:8
Then shall the Assyrian fall with the sword, not of a mighty man; and the sword, not of a mean man, shall devour him: but he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be discomfited.
corruption_summary: Not redefined by controversy but weakened by usage—the battlefield rout has dwindled to mere embarrassment; the word recovers the LORD’s mighty undoing of His enemies and the assurance that the battle is His.
corruption_paragraphs: The living corruption of discomfit is not ideological but a shrinking of sense that mirrors a shrinking of faith. In modern speech to be discomfited is merely to be flustered, mildly embarrassed, put slightly ill at ease—a word for social awkwardness. But in Scripture it is the LORD un-making an army: Amalek routed, Sisera’s nine hundred chariots scattered, the Assyrian host devoured by no human sword. The weakening of the word tracks the age’s loss of the God of hosts who fights for His people, the God who scatters His enemies with arrows and lightning. Where men no longer believe in a Lord who discomfits the proud, the word itself decays into a synonym for embarrassment. Recover the strong sense, and you recover the strong God behind it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the rout of God’s enemies is God’s own work. Joshua wielded the sword, but Moses’ uplifted hands held the victory; Barak charged, but the LORD discomfited Sisera; David’s song gives the glory to the arrows and lightning of heaven, not to the arm of flesh. The Church does not conquer by her own strength, nor is she to fear the chariots and hosts arrayed against her. The battle is the LORD’s; the enemy He undertakes to discomfit is undone indeed, and the gates of hell shall not prevail. Fight, then, under uplifted hands of intercession, and leave the discomfiting to the God of hosts.
roots_summary: Old French desconfire / Latin dis- + conficere (to un-make, finish off) — to rout, overthrow in battle; rendering Hebrew hāmam, the LORD’s confounding of His enemies.
roots_lines: Latin dis- + conficere — to un-do, un-make, finish off; the literal picture of an enemy accomplished and undone.
Old French desconfire — to defeat, destroy, rout; its past participle desconfit passing into English as the verb.
Hebrew hāmam (H2000) — to rout, confuse, throw into panic (Exo 14:24; Jos 10:10; Jdg 4:15, the LORD discomfiting Sisera).
Hebrew chāthath / kāthath — kindred verbs of breaking and dismaying an enemy host (Isa 31:8; Num 14:45).
English comfit, confect — the positive cousins from conficere (to make up), now surviving mainly in the sweet-maker’s craft.
usage: Joshua discomfited Amalek—yet the sword below prevailed only while Moses’ hands were held up on the hill; the rout was won by intercession as much as by steel.
The LORD discomfited Sisera, and all his chariots: nine hundred chariots of iron scattered, and the captain fleeing away on his feet before Barak.
The modern ear hears only embarrassment in discomfit; the KJV means a battlefield rout—the God of hosts un-making an army with arrows and lightning.

etymology: The past tense of the old verb to pill, from Old English / Old French peler (Latin pilare, to strip of hair; pellis, skin), “to peel, to strip off the bark or rind.” The same word as modern peel; in the KJV it renders Hebrew pātsal, to peel or strip.
biblical_def: To pill is to peel, to strip off the bark or rind—the identical word as peel, only in its older spelling. It belongs to the strange account of Jacob’s husbandry in Laban’s service: Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods (Gen 30:37). He then set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters at the watering troughs (Gen 30:38), that the cattle conceiving before the peeled rods should bring forth ringstraked and speckled young—the very sort agreed upon as his wages. The peeling laid bare the white beneath the bark, a device of striped and mottled rods before the mating flocks. Yet the passage must be read to its end, for Jacob himself later confesses that it was no magic in the rods but the God of Bethel who prospered him: God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me (Gen 31:9), and the ringstraked increase came by a dream and a divine hand, not by poplar bark. So the pilled rods stand as a monument to providence working through, and beyond, the schemes of men. Jacob pilled his rods and laid his plans, and God—who needs no rods—kept His covenant, turning even Laban’s fraud to the multiplying of the promised seed.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PILL as to peel; to strip off the bark, rind, or skin; the older form of the verb now spelled peel.
webster_full: PILL, v.t. — To peel; to strip off the bark, rind, or outer coat; to lay bare what lies beneath the covering. Jacob... pilled white strakes in them (Gen 30:37).
PILL, v.t. — To strip; to remove the covering of a thing, as bark from a rod or skin from fruit.
PILL, v.t. — Formerly also, to plunder or pillage; to strip a people of their goods (a kindred sense now obsolete).
PILLED, pp. — Peeled; stripped of bark or rind; laid bare, as the white strakes in Jacob’s rods.
PILLING, ppr. — Peeling; stripping off the outer coat or covering; the older spelling of peeling.
scriptures: And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods.
And he set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters in the watering troughs when the flocks came to drink, that they should conceive when they came to drink.
And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted.
And it came to pass at the time that the cattle conceived, that I lifted up mine eyes, and saw in a dream, and, behold, the rams which leaped upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled.
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine under dispute but a plain old word for peeling; it recovers the truth that providence, not the schemer’s device, prospers the covenant seed—God keeping His promise even through Jacob’s peeled rods.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the passage rebukes is the ancient one of trusting the device rather than the God who honours the promise. Jacob pilled his rods and contrived his stratagem, and a superstitious reading has always been tempted to credit the striped poplar with the striped lambs—as if the peeling itself worked the increase. But Jacob himself corrects us: it was a dream from the God of Bethel, and the plain word God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me. The age loves its own peeled rods—its techniques, its leverage, its clever management of outcomes—and forgets the hand that alone gives the increase. The pilled rods stand as a quiet rebuke to every confidence in method over the Master, in the scheme over the sovereign LORD who prospers whom He will.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is providence overruling the schemes of men to keep covenant. Jacob was a schemer, and his peeled rods were the device of a man still learning to trust; yet God had promised to bless him, and God did bless him—not because the rods availed, but because the covenant held. The ringstraked flocks were the LORD’s gift, given by a dream, wrung even out of Laban’s long fraud. So the believer may lay his plans and use his means, but let him ascribe the increase where Jacob at last ascribed it: to the God of Bethel, who keeps His word to the seed of promise whether the rods be peeled or no.
roots_summary: Old English / Old French peler, Latin pilare (to strip) — to peel, strip off bark; the older spelling of peel, rendering Hebrew pātsal in Jacob’s pilled rods.
roots_lines: Latin pilare — to deprive of hair, to strip (from pilus, a hair); and pellis, skin, behind the sense of stripping a surface.
Old French peler — to peel, strip off the skin or rind; passing into English as both pill and, later, peel.
Hebrew pātsal (H6478) — to peel, strip off (Gen 30:37, 38, of Jacob pilling the white strakes in the rods).
Hebrew pātsal — its noun kin petsel, a peeling or strip, marking the laid-bare white of the rod.
English peel — the surviving modern form of the same verb, keeping the exact sense of pilling.
usage: Jacob... pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear—the old spelling of peeled; he stripped the bark to lay bare the white beneath.
The pilled rods were Jacob’s device, but the ringstraked increase came by a dream from the God of Bethel—providence, not poplar bark, prospered the covenant seed.
The age trusts its own peeled rods—its techniques and leverage—and forgets the hand that gives the increase; Jacob learned to ascribe the flocks to the LORD.

etymology: A compound of ring and straked (streaked), from Old English hring (ring, circle) + strica (a stroke, streak, line): marked with rings or encircling streaks. In the KJV it describes the ringed and streaked cattle of Jacob’s wages, rendering Hebrew 'āqod, striped or banded.
biblical_def: Ringstraked means marked with rings or encircling bands of colour—striped, banded, streaked round about—and it is the peculiar word for the mottled cattle that became Jacob’s hire in Laban’s house. When the wages were set, Jacob removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted (Gen 30:35), and afterward the flocks brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted (Gen 30:39). The colour of the beasts became the very ledger of the covenant, for Laban shifted the terms again and again: If he said thus, The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked (Gen 31:8). Whatever Laban named as Jacob’s wage, that the flocks bore, until it was plain that no cunning of Jacob’s and no fraud of Laban’s governed the increase, but the God of Bethel: I lifted up mine eyes, and saw in a dream, and, behold, the rams which leaped upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled (Gen 31:10). The ringstraked cattle are therefore a parable of providence writ in wool and hide. Laban meant to defraud; God meant to bless; and the striped and speckled flocks multiplied under the eye of the LORD who had promised Jacob at Bethel to keep him and bring him again. The believer’s wages are safe in such a hand: the God who could make the cattle bear whatever colour His covenant required can make all things serve the good of His own.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RINGSTRAKED (ring-streaked) as having circular streaks or lines on the body; marked with bands or rings of differing colour.
webster_full: RINGSTRAKED, a. — Having circular streaks or lines on the body; marked with rings or bands of differing colour. The he goats that were ringstraked and spotted (Gen 30:35).
RINGSTRAKED, a. — Streaked around, as a beast whose coat is banded with encircling stripes.
RINGSTRAKED, a. — Written also RINGSTREAKED; the older form retaining strake for streak.
STRAKE, n. — A streak, stripe, or line of colour; an old form of streak, surviving in this compound.
RING, n. — A circle, or that which encircles; here the encircling band of colour marking the beast.
scriptures: And he removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted, and all the she goats that were speckled and spotted, and every one that had some white in it, and all the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons.
And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted.
Gen 31:8
If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages; then all the cattle bare speckled: and if he said thus, The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked.
And it came to pass at the time that the cattle conceived, that I lifted up mine eyes, and saw in a dream, and, behold, the rams which leaped upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a vivid old word for banded cattle; it recovers the providence of God over Jacob’s wages—the LORD making the very colour of the flocks serve His covenant against Laban’s fraud.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the fretful unbelief that thinks a man’s wages lie at the mercy of a defrauding master. Laban changed Jacob’s wages ten times, naming now the speckled and now the ringstraked as his hire, always seeking to leave him the barest portion. The age knows Laban well—the shifting bargain, the moved goalpost, the employer or circumstance that seems to hold a man’s living in its grip. But the ringstraked cattle answer the fret: whatever Laban named, the flocks bore, for the increase was not in Laban’s power nor in Jacob’s craft but in the hand of the God of Bethel. The striped and speckled beasts are a rebuke to anxious scheming and a comfort to honest labour under a hard master: the LORD can make the very wombs of the flock serve the wages He has appointed for His own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over a believer’s provision. Jacob had a promise from Bethel—I am with thee, and will keep thee—and that promise held through twenty years of Laban’s cheating, cashed out at last in ringstraked and speckled flocks. God did not spare Jacob the hard master, but He overruled the hard master to the keeping of His word. So the Christian need not fret over the Labans of his life; the God who could dictate the colour of the cattle can order every circumstance of his wages and his welfare to the good He has purposed, and none can defraud the man whom the LORD has undertaken to bless.
roots_summary: Old English hring (ring) + strica (streak) — marked with encircling bands; rendering Hebrew 'āqod (striped), the banded cattle of Jacob’s providentially guarded wages.
roots_lines: Old English hring — a ring, circle, or that which encircles; the first element of the compound.
Old English strica — a stroke, streak, or line; surviving as strake/streak in the second element.
Hebrew 'āqod (H6124) — striped, banded, ringstraked (Gen 30:35, 39; 31:8, 10, 12, of Jacob’s cattle).
Hebrew nāqod (H5348) — speckled, spotted (the companion term, Gen 30:32-33), naming the other markings of the flock.
English streak, strake — the surviving forms of the second element, keeping the sense of a line or band of colour.
usage: The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked—whatever Laban named as Jacob’s wage, the flocks bore, for God ruled the increase.
The ringstraked cattle are a parable of providence writ in wool and hide: Laban meant to defraud, God meant to bless, and the striped flocks multiplied under the LORD’s eye.
The believer need not fret over the Labans of his life; the God who dictated the colour of the cattle can order every circumstance of his wages to the good He has purposed.

etymology: A worn-down form of appurtenance, from Old French apartenance (that which pertains or belongs to a thing), Latin appertinere (to pertain, belong to): here the inner parts “belonging” to the carcase—the pluck, the heart, liver, and entrails. It renders the Hebrew qereb, the inward parts.
biblical_def: The purtenance is the inward parts of a beast—the pluck, the heart, liver, and entrails that pertain or belong to the body—and the word stands but once in the KJV, in the law of the passover: the lamb is to be roast with fire, his head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof (Exo 12:9). Nothing of the lamb was to be sodden in water nor eaten raw, but the whole—head, legs, and inwards together—was to pass through the fire and be eaten in the night of redemption. The command is emphatic and total: the lamb was to be taken entire, its inward parts not discarded but roasted with the rest, that the household might feed upon the whole sacrifice with nothing left over till the morning (Exo 12:8, 10). The purtenance thus guards a great gospel figure. Christ is our passover, sacrificed for us (1Co 5:7); and as the passover lamb was given whole to the fire and whole to the eating, so the whole Christ is given for His people and received by them—not a Saviour parcelled out, not His hard sayings left on the plate, not His lordship divided from His mercy. The fire that consumed the offering (Lev 1:9) is the figure of the wrath He bore entire; the eating is the faith that feeds on the whole Christ. Nothing of the Lamb is to be left uneaten: head, legs, and purtenance, the whole of Him is our food and our salvation.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PURTENANCE as the pluck of an animal; the inwards or intestines; a corruption of appurtenance.
webster_full: PURTENANCE, n. — The pluck of an animal; the inwards or intestines; the heart, liver, and entrails. His head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof (Exo 12:9).
PURTENANCE, n. — That which pertains or belongs to the carcase; the inner parts appurtenant to the body of the beast.
PURTENANCE, n. — A worn form of APPURTENANCE, retaining the sense of things belonging to a whole.
APPURTENANCE, n. — That which belongs or pertains to something else; an adjunct or appendage; the parent word.
PURTENANCE — Now obsolete except in the language of Scripture and old husbandry.
scriptures: Exo 12:9
Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire; his head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof.
Exo 12:8
And they shall eat the flesh in that night, roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs they shall eat it.
Lev 1:9
But his inwards and his legs shall he wash in water: and the priest shall burn all on the altar, to be a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD.
Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us:
corruption_summary: A KJV hapax of the passover, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the wholeness of the sacrifice—the whole Lamb given to the fire and to the eating, figuring the whole Christ received entire by faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the modern appetite for a parcelled Christ—a Saviour taken in pieces, His comforts kept and His commands declined, His mercy relished and His lordship left on the plate. The passover would have none of it: head, legs, and purtenance, the whole lamb went to the fire and the whole lamb was eaten, and nothing was to remain till the morning. The age loves to choose among the inward parts of the faith, to keep the palatable and discard the purtenance—the hard sayings, the cost, the cross. But a lamb divided is no passover, and a Christ divided is no Saviour. The command that nothing of the Lamb be left uneaten is a standing rebuke to every selective, self-flattering religion that would feed on the Redeemer’s benefits while refusing His yoke.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wholeness of Christ given and received. As the passover lamb was roast entire and eaten entire, so the whole Christ—Prophet, Priest, and King; His atoning death and His righteous rule; His sweet promises and His searching demands—is offered to sinners and is to be received by faith without reserve. Christ our passover is sacrificed for us; let us keep the feast, not with the old leaven of a divided allegiance, but feeding on the whole Lamb. Nothing of Him is to be left over; head, legs, and purtenance, He is wholly ours, and we are to be wholly His.
roots_summary: Old French apartenance / Latin appertinere (to pertain, belong) — the inward parts belonging to the carcase; the KJV hapax at Exo 12:9, rendering Hebrew qereb, the inwards.
roots_lines: Latin appertinere — to pertain, belong to (from ad- + pertinere); the source of the sense of parts belonging to a whole.
Old French apartenance — that which pertains or belongs; worn down in English to purtenance.
Hebrew qereb (H7130) — the inward part, midst, entrails (Exo 12:9, the purtenance of the passover lamb; Lev 3:3).
Hebrew peder / kāved — the fat and the liver among the inwards, the choicest parts given to the fire (Lev 3:4).
English appurtenance, pertain — the surviving kin, keeping the sense of what belongs or is annexed to a thing.
usage: His head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof—the whole passover lamb, inward parts and all, was to pass through the fire and be eaten in the night of redemption.
As the lamb was given whole to the fire and whole to the eating, so the whole Christ is given and received—not a Saviour parcelled out, His hard sayings left on the plate.
Nothing of the Lamb was to be left uneaten; the command rebukes every selective religion that feeds on the Redeemer’s benefits while refusing His yoke.

etymology: From Old Norse skreppa and Old French escreppe, a wallet or small bag; kin to scrap, a small piece. A shepherd’s or traveller’s pouch for provisions. It renders Hebrew yālqūt (a shepherd’s bag) and Greek pēra (a traveller’s wallet).
biblical_def: A scrip is a small bag or wallet—the shepherd’s or pilgrim’s pouch, slung over the shoulder to carry a little bread or a few stones for the road. David bore one to the fight: he took his staff, and chose five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd’s bag which he had, even in a scrip (1Sa 17:40), and out of that humble pouch came the stone that felled Goliath. But the scrip gains its deepest weight in the sending of the Twelve and the Seventy, where the Lord commands them to go without it: nor scrip for your journey (Mat 10:10); no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse (Mar 6:8). To go without a scrip was to go without the traveller’s reserve, without the visible security of stored provision, cast wholly upon the God who sends and upon the households that would receive them, for the workman is worthy of his meat. And when the Lord afterward asked them to recount that mission, the scrip becomes a monument to His faithfulness: When I sent you without purse, and scrip, and shoes, lacked ye any thing? And they said, Nothing (Luk 22:35). The empty scrip preached a sermon the full one could not: that the servant sent by Christ shall not want, that provision follows obedience, and that the God who clothes the lilies will not fail the messenger of the gospel. To go scripless at His word is not recklessness but faith, and it lacked nothing.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SCRIP as a small bag; a wallet; a satchel, such as shepherds and pilgrims carried for provisions.
webster_full: SCRIP, n. — A small bag; a wallet; a satchel. Put them in a shepherd’s bag which he had, even in a scrip (1Sa 17:40).
SCRIP, n. — A traveller’s pouch for carrying bread or other provisions on a journey.
SCRIP, n. — (In a distinct sense) a small writing; a schedule; a certificate—from a different root, the Latin scriptum.
SCRIP, n. — The shepherd’s pouch, as distinguished from the purse for money and the staff for the way.
SCRIP — In the sense of a bag, now archaic, surviving chiefly in the language of Scripture and pastoral verse.
scriptures: And he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip; and his sling was in his hand: and he drew near to the Philistine.
Nor scrip for your journey, neither two coats, neither shoes, nor yet staves: for the workman is worthy of his meat.
Mar 6:8
And commanded them that they should take nothing for their journey, save a staff only; no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse.
And he said unto them, When I sent you without purse, and scrip, and shoes, lacked ye any thing? And they said, Nothing.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a homely old word for a bag; it recovers the faith of the scripless errand—the servant sent by Christ who lacks nothing, provision following obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: The empty scrip rebukes the age’s bondage to the stored reserve—the anxious heaping up of provision as the only imagined security, the settled unbelief that a man is safe only so far as his own bag is full. The Lord sent His messengers without scrip on purpose, that they might learn in their own bodies that the workman is worthy of his meat and that the God who sends provides. This is not a counsel of improvidence; it is a rebuke of the idolatry of the reserve, the quiet conviction that the full scrip, and not the sending Lord, is what keeps a man. The disciples went out with empty pouches and came back having lacked nothing, and the memory of it was to steady them for every future trial. The age that trusts its stored bag more than its living God needs the sermon of the empty scrip.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that provision follows obedience for the servant Christ has sent. When I sent you without purse, and scrip, and shoes, lacked ye any thing? Nothing. The Lord does not promise His messengers a full scrip, but He does promise that they shall not want; He appoints the households that receive them, moves the hearts that supply them, and honours the labour of His workmen with their meat. Let the servant of the gospel go where he is sent, whether with scrip or without, resting not in the pouch but in the Provider, and he shall find at the journey’s end that he lacked nothing at all.
roots_summary: Old Norse skreppa / Old French escreppe (a wallet) — a shepherd’s or traveller’s bag; rendering Hebrew yālqūt and Greek pēra, the pouch the sent servant could do without.
roots_lines: Old Norse skreppa — a scrip, wallet, or small bag; a chief source of the English word.
Old French escreppe — a pilgrim’s or beggar’s pouch; reinforcing the sense of a traveller’s bag.
Hebrew yālqūt (H3219) — a shepherd’s bag or receptacle (1Sa 17:40, David’s scrip for the five stones).
Greek pēra (G4082) — a leather pouch or wallet for provisions (Mat 10:10; Mar 6:8; Luk 9:3; 10:4; 22:35).
English scrap — a native cousin, keeping the sense of a small piece such as a small bag might hold.
usage: David put them in a shepherd’s bag which he had, even in a scrip—out of that humble pouch came the smooth stone that felled Goliath.
The Lord sent the Twelve with no scrip, no bread, no money, that they might learn the workman is worthy of his meat and the sending God provides.
When I sent you without... scrip... lacked ye any thing? Nothing—the empty scrip preached the sermon the full one could not: the servant of Christ shall not want.

etymology: From Old English cēapman, a trader or dealer, from cēap (trade, bargain, price—the root also of cheap and chaffer) + man: a man of trade, a merchant or peddler. It renders the Hebrew participle of trafficking men who traded with Solomon.
biblical_def: A chapman is a trader, a dealer, a travelling merchant—a man of cheap in its old sense of trade and bargain. The word appears but once in the KJV, in the account of Solomon’s golden splendour: the yearly weight of gold that came to him was besides that which chapmen and merchants brought (2Ch 9:14), the traders and dealers whose caravans, with the kings of Arabia and the governors of the country, poured gold and silver into Jerusalem. The chapmen figure the reach of Solomon’s peace and wisdom, when the nations came bringing tribute to the son of David on his throne—a shadow, dim but real, of a greater Son of David to whom the kings shall bring presents and all nations serve. Scripture knows the merchant in many places: the virtuous woman maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant (Pro 31:24), honest trade as a fruit of diligence; and the kingdom of heaven is likened to a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls, who sold all he had to buy the one of great price (Mat 13:45). Yet the trader can also stand for the world under judgment: the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over fallen Babylon (Rev 18:11), when their traffic in her luxuries comes to nothing in a day. The chapman thus teaches a double lesson: lawful commerce is a good gift, and the wealth of nations may serve the throne of the true Solomon; but the merchant who lays up treasure in Babylon, and not in the pearl of great price, shall mourn when her market fails.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CHAPMAN as a cheapener; one who offers as a purchaser; a market-man; a buyer or seller; a trader.
webster_full: CHAPMAN, n. — A cheapener; one that offers as a purchaser; a buyer; a trader. Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought (2Ch 9:14).
CHAPMAN, n. — A market-man; a dealer in goods; one who buys and sells; a peddler or itinerant trader.
CHAPMAN, n. — One who chaffers or bargains; from the old sense of cheap, trade or price.
CHAP, v. — To cheapen; to bargain; to chaffer—the root verb, now obsolete, behind the trader’s name.
CHAPMEN, n. plur. — Traders; dealers; those who traffic in merchandise, as the chapmen who brought gold to Solomon.
scriptures: Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon.
She maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant.
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:
And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:
corruption_summary: A KJV hapax for a trader, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the double lesson of commerce—lawful trade as a good gift and a tribute to the true Solomon, yet a snare to the merchant who lays up his treasure in Babylon.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapman rebukes the age’s making of trade into a god. Commerce is a good gift: the chapmen brought their gold to Solomon, the virtuous woman sold her linen and girdles with honest diligence, and the merchant seeking goodly pearls became the Lord’s own figure for the soul that will part with all for the kingdom. But the same trading heart, unmoored from God, becomes the merchant of Babylon, weeping over a fallen market because his treasure was all in the merchandise that no man buys any more. The temptation is not to trade but to trust the trade—to reckon a man’s life by the abundance of his traffic, to buy and sell and get gain while laying up nothing toward God. The word sets the honest chapman beside the Babylonish merchant and asks where a man’s treasure truly lies.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that all lawful commerce is to serve the throne of the true Solomon and the seeking of the pearl of great price. The chapmen who brought gold to Solomon foreshadow the nations bringing their glory to Christ, to whom the kings shall bring presents and every knee shall bow. Let the believer trade honestly, sell his linen and deliver his girdles, and prosper as God gives—but let him be above all the merchant man who, finding one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had and bought it. The chapman who gains the whole world and loses that pearl has made the worst bargain of all; the wise trader buys the field for the treasure hid therein.
roots_summary: Old English cēapman (trader), from cēap (trade, bargain—root of cheap) + man — a merchant or dealer; the KJV hapax of the chapmen who brought gold to Solomon.
roots_lines: Old English cēap — trade, bargain, price; the root also of cheap and chaffer, naming the act of buying and selling.
Old English cēapman — a man of trade, merchant, or dealer; the compound behind the KJV word.
Hebrew tār / the participle of trafficking men (2Ch 9:14) — the traders and dealers who brought gold to Solomon.
Hebrew rākal / sōchēr (H5503) — to go about as a trader, to traffic; the common word for merchant (Pro 31:24; Eze 27).
English cheap, chaffer, chapbook — the surviving kin, all keeping the old sense of trade and bargaining.
usage: Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought—the traders whose caravans poured gold into Solomon’s Jerusalem, a shadow of the nations bringing tribute to the true Son of David.
The virtuous woman delivereth girdles unto the merchant: honest trade as a fruit of diligence, and a good gift of God rightly used.
The merchant of Babylon weeps when his market fails; the merchant man seeking goodly pearls sold all he had for the one of great price—the chapman must choose where his treasure lies.
